answers_by_date.basis: DL 1.094 Arts. 23 and 29 and DS 597 Arts. 35 and 49 (1998-2000 version read) let a holder of a contract-worker or temporary-resident visa extend it to 'the spouse, parents or children' as dependants, if they live with the holder or 'a sus expensas'. DS 597 Art. 102 No. 2 also treated the spouse and children of a resident or permanent resident as having family ties for a temporary visa. Only dependent nuclear family were covered, so 'Conditional'. I found no practice evidence for this period, so the rating carries over the 2020 level.

Same provisions. The only amendments since 2000 did not touch family members: Decreto 2910 (in force 23 May 2000) changed DS 597 Arts. 39, 40 and 47, and Ley 19.806 (in force 31 May 2002) changed DL 1.094 Arts. 56 and 68. I found no practice evidence for this period.

Same provisions; Ley 20.430 on refugees (in force 15 April 2010) came after this date. The UN migrant workers committee (CMW, 2011) found that 'in practice, some migrant workers face obstacles to family reunification' and noted 'the absence of a legal framework regulating family reunification'. That supports a rating between Rarely and Sometimes.

Same dependant regime under DL 1.094 and DS 597. Since 15 April 2010, Ley 20.430 Art. 9 has also let refugees' spouse or cohabiting partner, ascendants, descendants and wards obtain refugee status by extension. Decreto 1930 (in force 7 March 2015) came after this date and did not touch Arts. 35 or 49. Practice evidence is the CMW 2011 finding only; I found nothing documented for 2014-2015.

answers.change_2000_2020: There have been right protections both in 2000 and 2020 and neither the right protection nor the implementation level of these protections has changed

answers.sourcing_note: I read the DL 1.094 and DS 597 version tables on LeyChile and the DS 597 text in its 1998-2000 version, which was in force on 1 January 2000. The 2005, 2010 and 2015 texts are inferred from the version tables and amendment markers, which show no change to the family provisions. Practice evidence exists only for around 2010 (CMW 2011); PDFs (UDP annual reports) could not be read.
answers.notes: The protection answer is the same on every date: only dependent nuclear family (spouse, parents, children) of residence-visa holders could join them, by administrative extension of the holder's visa. The refugee track changed in 2010 (Ley 20.430 Art. 9 replaced DL 1.094's refugee provisions), but this does not change the answer for settled migrants. DL 1.094 and DS 597 were both repealed on 12 February 2022 by Ley 21.325 and Decreto 296, after the 2020 date. A 2018 executive measure (the humanitarian family-reunification visa for Haitians) lies outside the dates coded.

answers_by_date.basis: The constitutional protection action (Constitución Art. 20, 1980 text) let anyone, foreigners included, challenge an arbitrary or illegal act that affects listed Art. 19 rights before the Court of Appeals. DL 1.094 gave a specific judicial appeal only against expulsion (Art. 89, to the Supreme Court within 24 hours), not against a refused visa. The remedy is therefore indirect and depends on an Art. 19 right being affected. I found no practice evidence for this period.

Same provisions. Ley 20.050 (in force 26 August 2005, after this date) only rewrote Art. 20's second paragraph on the environment. Ley 19.880 (2003) added administrative remedies, not judicial ones. I found no practice evidence.

Art. 20 as amended in 2005 (environment paragraph only); DL 1.094 Art. 89 still covered expulsion only. In 2011 the CMW criticised how accessible appeals against expulsion were; that concerns expulsion, not visa refusals. I found no documented practice on protection actions against family-visa refusals.

Ley 20.516 (in force 11 July 2011) added Art. 19 No. 3 paragraph 5 (right to legal defence) to the rights protected by the action; it does not change how a visa refusal can be challenged. The framework is otherwise the same. I found no practice evidence read for this period; the rating carries over the 2020 level.

answers.change_2000_2020: There have been right protections both in 2000 and 2020 and neither the right protection nor the implementation level of these protections has changed

answers_by_date.basis: DS 597 Arts. 35 and 49 extend visas only to the 'cónyuge'. Under Chilean law marriage was between a man and a woman, and no instrument recognised same-sex unions. I found no practice of recognising same-sex partners.
Same provisions; no same-sex recognition in force.

Same provisions. Ley 20.430 Art. 9 (in force April 2010, after this date) speaks of a refugee's cohabiting partner ('persona con la cual se halle ligado por razón de convivencia'); it was not in force on 1 January 2010 and is not marriage recognition.

The civil union law, Ley 20.830 (published 21 April 2015, in force 22 October 2015), was not yet in force. Its Art. 12 later recognised foreign same-sex marriages as civil unions; that is the event that explains the 2020 'Yes'.

answers.change_2000_2020: There was no right protection (as of January 1, 2000), but there is now (as of January 1, 2020)

answers.sourcing_note: I read the DS 597 versions for 2000 and later, and Ley 20.830's original version with its entry-into-force rule. I did not find or read any DEM circular extending dependant visas to civil partners.
answers.starting_answer_concern: The 2020 'Yes' cites Ley 21.325 Art. 19, which was not in force until February 2022. In 2020 recognition rested only on Ley 20.830 Art. 12: a same-sex marriage counted as a civil union, not a marriage, and the DS 597 dependant provisions still said 'cónyuge'. Any extension to civil partners came from administrative practice that I could not verify. 'Conditional' may fit 2020 better; same-sex marriage itself came only with Ley 21.400 (in force March 2022).
answers.notes: The protection begins on 22 October 2015, between the 2015 and 2020 dates. The partner rule in Ley 20.430 Art. 9 (2010) is only for refugees and covers cohabitation, not marriage, so it does not make the 2010-2015 answers 'Yes'.

answers_by_date.basis: In the 1998-2000 DS 597 text, Art. 15(a) required residence-visa applicants to document 'solvencia económica', and Arts. 35/49 limit family visas to dependants who live 'a expensas del titular'. DL 1.094 Art. 15 No. 4 barred entry to those without the 'recursos que les permitan vivir en Chile sin constituir carga social'. Reunification was therefore conditioned on resources.
Same provisions; no amendment to DS 597 Arts. 15, 35 or 49, or to DL 1.094 Art. 15 No. 4.
Same provisions. Ley 20.430 (April 2010, after this date) later set no resource test for refugees' families, only a dependency test, but it covers refugees only.

Same provisions for migrants. Ley 20.507 (2011) changed only DL 1.094 Art. 15 No. 2, not No. 4. Refugees' families have been extended status under Ley 20.430 Art. 9 without income conditions since 2010, but the indicator concerns migrants generally.

answers.change_2000_2020: There have been no right protections neither in 2000 nor in 2020

answers.repealed_search: I searched for a resource-free family route for migrants that existed between 2000 and 2020 and was later repealed. I compared the DS 597 version in force 1998-2000 with later versions (Arts. 15, 35, 49, 102) and checked the DL 1.094 version table (amendments 2002, 2010, 2011). The 'solvencia económica' and 'a expensas' requirements are present in every version, and no repealed protection was found. The only resource-free family route is the refugee extension in Ley 20.430 Art. 9 (from 2010), which is still in force.
answers.sourcing_note: I read the DS 597 text in force on 1 January 2000 and the later consolidated text, and the DL 1.094 text with its amendment markers. I read no practice sources; the answer is 'No' throughout, so implementation is Does Not Apply.
answers.notes: The 2020 citation ('protects this right in Art. 19 of Law 21325') contradicts its own 'No' answer, and cites a law not in force in 2020. The 'No' for 2020 is supported by the DS 597 and DL 1.094 provisions above.
